scope: The existing anchored knowledge catalogue, not the complete guideline

cases.text: Blood pressure is consistently 175 systolic and 105 diastolic despite treatment.
Antihypertensive therapy has controlled blood pressure over four weeks with no driving-impairing side effects or relevant target-organ damage.
Persistent systolic blood pressure is exactly 170 mmHg; persistent diastolic blood pressure is exactly 100 mmHg.
One blood pressure reading is elevated; persistent hypertension has not been established.
Uncorrected visual acuity is 6/12 in the better eye and 6/24 in the worse eye.
The binocular visual field extends 140 degrees and the field loss is static with no significant scotoma.
No diplopia within 20 degrees of central fixation is reported.
The driver is monocular with visual acuity of 6/9 in the remaining eye.
Initial clinical hearing assessment suggests hearing loss; audiometry is required.
Unaided hearing loss in the better ear averages exactly 40 dB across 500, 1000, 2000 and 3000 Hz.
The driver uses hearing aids; an audiologist is assessing hearing for a conditional licence.
Hearing screening suggests impairment, but no audiogram is available.
The mechanism of transient loss of consciousness remains under investigation; cardiovascular and neurological investigations are pending and a diagnosis is not established.
Vasovagal syncope occurred during venepuncture with a well-defined provoking factor unlikely to recur while driving.
A single blackout of undetermined nature occurred three years ago.
Two unexplained blackouts separated by more than 24 hours occurred seven years ago.
The blackout has a firm diagnosis of hypoglycaemia and should be assessed against the relevant condition standard.
Diabetes is managed by diet and exercise alone without medication.
Diabetes is treated with insulin.
An insulin-treated driver had a recent severe hypoglycaemic event and needs specialist review before returning to driving.
The driver is acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes and acute hyperglycaemia.
An insulin-treated commercial driver presents three months of blood glucose monitoring records for endocrinologist review.
